record.paper_title: An Overview of Compact Star Populations and Some of Its Open Problems
record.original_question: Does the compact-object mass distribution contain a true lower black-hole mass gap between about 2 and 5 solar masses, or is that interval only partially depleted, with some objects and formation channels populating at least part of the 2.5–5 solar-mass range?

evidence.quote: its existence has remained an open question for over 20 years
The gap has been connected to the characteristic convection timescale in core-collapse supernovae [26,27], but even in this case a partial filling has not been ruled out.

It seems thus clear at this point that, if there is a gap, it should not start below ∼2.5 M☉, and that the investigation of alternative formation channels for compact objects is needed to further constrain the degree to which the 2.5–5 M☉ range is populated.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the mass distribution of stellar-mass compact remnants (neutron stars and black holes) formed via stellar evolution and observed through electromagnetic and gravitational-wave channels. Empirically, neutron-star masses cluster below roughly 2.5 solar masses while observed stellar black holes are typically found at or above about 5 solar masses, suggesting a possible "lower mass gap" in the interval from approximately 2 to 5 solar masses (or, more conservatively, 2.5 to 5 solar masses).

Question: Does the underlying compact-object mass distribution contain a true gap in the interval [2, 5] solar masses (equivalently, is this interval essentially unpopulated), or is the interval only partially depleted, in the sense that there exist compact objects, formed through standard or alternative formation channels (such as core-collapse supernovae with different convective timescales, binary interactions, accretion-induced collapse, or hierarchical/dynamical processes), whose masses lie within the 2.5–5 solar-mass range with non-negligible probability? In particular, determine (i) whether a strict gap exists, (ii) if not, the lower edge above which any depletion begins, and (iii) the formation channels capable of populating the 2.5–5 solar-mass range.
artifact.status_search_result: The existence and structure of the lower black-hole mass gap (roughly 2–5 solar masses) remains an active and unresolved question. Recent gravitational-wave detections such as GW190425 and GW230529, together with electromagnetic discoveries of mass-gap candidates in wide binaries (e.g., the 2024 Nature Astronomy report), have produced objects with masses inside the putative gap, shifting debate toward whether the gap is real but partially filled or absent altogether. As of 2025–2026, the literature still treats the question as open.

status_evidence.title: A potential mass-gap black hole in a wide binary with a circular orbit
status_evidence.snippet: Report of a compact object with mass within the putative 2.5–5 solar-mass lower mass gap, challenging a strict-gap interpretation.
status_evidence.claim: Observational evidence indicates at least partial filling of the lower mass gap, but a definitive determination of the gap's existence is not established.

status_evidence.title: Cut from a different cloth: Binary black holes in the mass gap (astrobites)
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses ongoing flexible population modelling of binary black holes around the mass gaps as of 2025.
status_evidence.claim: The community continues to model and debate the structure of the mass gap, indicating the problem remains open.

status_evidence.title: The Smallest Black Holes and Biggest Neutron Stars (astrobites)
status_evidence.snippet: GW230529 shifts the conversation from whether objects exist in the mass gap to how objects exist in the mass gap.
status_evidence.claim: The question of whether the gap is real or only partially depleted is still being debated.
